disease.inheritance: Autosomal dominant — TTR mutations (e.g. Val30Met, the most common)
disease.mechanism: Gain-of-function / toxic aggregate. Mutant transthyretin (TTR) is destabilized and misfolds, dissociating from its native homotetramer and aggregating into amyloid fibrils that deposit in peripheral nerves and heart. This causes progressive sensorimotor/autonomic neuropathy and infiltrative cardiomyopathy. The amyloidogenic TTR is the toxic species.
disease.autotac_rationale: ELIGIBLE. Amyloidogenic TTR is a toxic gain-of-function aggregate — reducing or degrading the misfolded TTR is mechanistically appropriate. Approved therapies (patisiran, inotersen) already work by *silencing* TTR production; a selective degrader of amyloidogenic TTR is the same logic via a different route.
disease.prevalence: ~1 in 100,000 (Val30Met endemic in Portugal/Sweden/Japan; higher there) — commonly cited; UNVERIFIED exact figure this session
disease.age_of_onset: Adult onset (typically 30-70 years; earlier in endemic Val30Met regions)

approved_treatments.mechanism_correct: A small interfering RNA (siRNA) that degrades TTR mRNA, reducing hepatic transthyretin production and thereby lowering amyloidogenic TTR levels. It is NOT a small molecule and does not degrade the protein directly.
approved_treatments.note: NOTE: patisiran is an siRNA (~14 kDa duplex), not a small molecule — MW/PubChem CID left 0 to avoid fabrication. First-in-class RNAi therapy.

investigational: TTR stabilizers: tafamidis (Vyndaqel) — binds native tetramer, prevents dissociation (approved 2019)
CRISPR/Cas9 in vivo TTR gene editing (clinical, e.g. NTLA-2001)

disease.human_summary: Hereditary transthyretin amyloidosis is an autosomal dominant disease in which mutant transthyretin misfolds and forms amyloid deposits in nerves and heart, causing progressive neuropathy and cardiomyopathy. It is a toxic gain-of-function amyloidosis; approved therapies silence or stabilise the amyloidogenic protein, and selective degraders are the next frontier.
